rationale: Table 2 shows hallucination history in 53.3% of Parkinson fallers and 37.5% of nonfallers. Methods mention visual hallucinations. The study's outcome is falls and fractures and the exposure comparison does not measure dried figs.

The study compared complex I in brain samples from 10 Parkinson and 12 control donors. The clinical table records visual hallucinations in one donor with seizures. It does not systematically measure visual recurrence or culinary fig exposure.

The review discusses visual modality, vivid dreams and drug response evidence. It cites overlapping hallucination and illusion categories and distinct uncontrolled treatment trials. These are cited observations and no dried-fig comparison.

Hallucinations are documented in 10/24 with amygdala Lewy bodies and 9/30 without, using item-specific chart denominators and undifferentiated modality. The study gives no significant contrast or fig exposure.

The review names visual hallucinations as a symptom of Lewy body dementia and describes diagnostic imaging patterns. No new visual comparison is measured. Figures are scan illustrations and the review does not assess figs.

The 16 Alzheimer cases and 16 controls were compared on receptor and perfusion tracer scans. The discussion mentions other visual hallucination evidence. The original comparison lacks Parkinson visual events and fig exposure.

The case reports on pages 243, 252 and 279 describe biochemical disturbance with visual symptoms, diagnosis revised to progressive supranuclear palsy, and visual impairment with Charles Bonnet syndrome, respectively. Figures are illustrations. No member supplies a dried-fig contrast for Parkinson visual frequency.
